text: The Halvren Institute of Tidal Engineering is a research institute based in Port Ossery. It was founded in 1987 by the engineer Mirela Danthorpe to study how tidal currents could be turned into electricity. The institute runs laboratories on the Port Ossery waterfront and field stations along the Varn Strait. Its best-known project is the Kestrel Tidal Array. The institute is funded by public grants and by licensing fees from its turbine designs.
title: Halvren Institute of Tidal Engineering

text: Mirela Danthorpe is an engineer known for her work on underwater turbines. She studied mechanical engineering at Quellmoor University, where she wrote a thesis on the fatigue of submerged blades. After graduating she spent several years as a consultant on harbour construction projects. In 1987 she moved to Port Ossery to set up her own research organisation, and in 2009 she stepped back from administration to return to design work.
title: Mirela Danthorpe

text: Quellmoor University is a public university in the city of Brindlehaven. It was established in 1891 and is organised into eleven faculties, including a faculty of engineering with a marine technology department. The main campus sits on the northern bank of the Ammer River. Quellmoor University is the second largest employer in Brindlehaven after the port.
title: Quellmoor University

text: The Kestrel Tidal Array is a tidal power station in the Varn Strait. It was designed and built by the Halvren Institute of Tidal Engineering and was commissioned in 2014. The array consists of twenty-four seabed turbines with a combined capacity of 42 megawatts, enough to supply roughly 30,000 homes. Power from the array is carried by an undersea cable to a substation near Port Ossery.
title: Kestrel Tidal Array

text: The Halvren Institute of Tidal Engineering has had three directors. Its founder led it from 1987 until 2009. Tobin Arkwright, a former naval engineer, was director from 2009 to 2018 and oversaw the construction of the institute's largest project. In 2018 Arkwright was succeeded by Ysolde Fenwick, who had previously led the Saltmarsh Observatory for eight years. Fenwick remains director today.
title: Leadership of the Halvren Institute

text: Orrex Maritime is a marine engineering company headquartered in Brindlehaven. It was founded in 1974 by the shipbuilder Caspar Orrex. The company began by building cargo barges and moved into offshore energy in the 1990s. Orrex Maritime built and operates the Lumen Bay Tidal Array and supplies foundations for offshore wind farms.
title: Orrex Maritime

text: The Lumen Bay Tidal Array is a tidal power station in Lumen Bay, south of Brindlehaven. It was built by Orrex Maritime and commissioned in 2011. The array has sixteen turbines with a combined capacity of 30 megawatts. It was the first commercial tidal array in the region, and its turbine foundations were later reused as a model for offshore wind projects.
title: Lumen Bay Tidal Array

text: Port Ossery is a harbour city on the eastern shore of the Varn Strait with a population of about 210,000. The economy of the city is based on fishing, ship repair and marine research. A ferry link connects Port Ossery with Corrin Isle, and the old harbour district is a popular destination for visitors in summer.
title: Port Ossery

text: The Saltmarsh Observatory is a coastal research station on Corrin Isle, at the northern mouth of the Varn Strait. It was established in 1962 to monitor tides and seabirds. Today the observatory studies how human activity affects marine wildlife in the strait. Ysolde Fenwick directed the observatory from 2010 to 2018.
title: Saltmarsh Observatory

text: Wren Calloway is a marine biologist at the Saltmarsh Observatory who studies grey seals. Between 2014 and 2017 she tracked seal colonies near the Kestrel Tidal Array to measure whether the turbines changed their feeding routes. She found that seals kept their distance from the turbines but that their feeding success was unchanged. Her results were published in 2017 in the book Currents and Colonies.
title: Wren Calloway

text: The Ossery Accord was an agreement signed in 1999 between the Halvren Institute of Tidal Engineering and Orrex Maritime. Under the accord the two organisations shared tidal current measurements and turbine performance data. The accord ended in 2016 after a dispute over access to performance data from the Kestrel Tidal Array, and since then the two organisations have operated as competitors.
title: Ossery Accord

text: Brindlehaven is the largest city in the region, with a population of about 480,000. It lies at the mouth of the Ammer River, where a deep-water port handles most of the regional cargo traffic. The city is governed by an elected council of thirty-one members and is known for its covered markets.
title: Brindlehaven

text: Kestrel Ridge is a granite ridge in the uplands west of Brindlehaven, named after the kestrels that nest on its cliffs. Its highest point reaches 1,140 metres. A restoration of the hiking trails on the ridge was completed in 2015 at a cost of 3 million crowns.
title: Kestrel Ridge

text: The Ossery Harbour Festival is an annual summer festival in Port Ossery, first held in 1952. It features boat races, a seafood market and a lantern procession along the old harbour. The festival has been cancelled only once, in 1988, because of a severe storm.
title: Ossery Harbour Festival

text: The Quellmoor Conservatory is the music school of Quellmoor University. It opened in 1923 and trains performers and composers. Its best-known graduate is the cellist Anja Merrow, who founded the Ammer String Quartet in 1961.
title: Quellmoor Conservatory

text: The Corrin Isle Lighthouse stands on the southern cliffs of Corrin Isle. It was built in 1874 and automated in 1979, when the last keeper left the island. The former keeper's cottage now houses a small museum about shipwrecks in the strait.
title: Corrin Isle Lighthouse

text: Orrex Ferries was a passenger ferry service between Brindlehaven and Corrin Isle. It was spun off from Orrex Maritime in 2003 and sold to Brindle Lines in 2012. The service used three vessels and carried about 400,000 passengers a year at its peak.
title: Orrex Ferries
